meaning.evidence: Every fact survives, as the text is close to verbatim: "Henry Ford's first large venture in his already announced campaign", the twenty-one quadrilles, the vaudeville contract, Tex Rickard. Ford's quote is kept word for word. "brand-spankin'-new Madison Square Garden" is colour on 'new'.

sense.evidence: The few swaps mostly fit: "he really reckoned" for thought, "with the missus" for with his wife, "will front up in New York" for arrive. "was to 'ave appeared" is a dropped h, not a term, and not an Australian one.

authenticity.evidence: Little Aussie and some of it off: "was to 'ave appeared" is a Cockney-style dropped h, "their teachin'" a lone dropped g in formal prose. "brand-spankin'-new" is bolted on.

register.evidence: Largely untranslated AP prose: "For this occasion Mr. Ford is advertising for couples to dance the square dance and to form a nucleus for the party." Far under a level-5 brief.

tone.evidence: The wire-report tone is intact because the text is barely changed: "It was reported last night that he'll be under the management of Tex Rickard".

flow.evidence: Reads as the original, but the insertions jar: "was to 'ave appeared at the Tuesday night affair", "to simplify their teachin' and encourage their popularity".

variety.evidence: Only a handful of swaps ("reckoned", "the missus", "front up", "brand-spankin'-new"); nothing repeated, but almost nothing there.

essence.evidence: It is the original story, shape and all: ""Mellie" Dunham, the champion fiddler of Maine" opens the second half as before.

problems.quote: For this occasion Mr. Ford is advertising for couples to dance the square dance and to form a nucleus for the party.
problems.original: For this occasion Mr. Ford is advertising for couples to dance the square dance and to form a nucleus for the party.
problems.why: Left untranslated, like most of the text; far lighter than a level-5 brief.
Dropped h is Cockney stage dialect, not Australian speech.

A.summary: A rule-engine pass: nearly verbatim, with a few insertions, one of them un-Australian.

meaning.evidence: Every fact survives: the campaign, the Tuesday dance, couples as the core, the four of twenty-one quadrilles, Mellie's week as guest, the change of plans, Tex Rickard's barn dance. Ford's quote is kept verbatim. "Henry Ford's already let on he's on a mission" renders 'already announced campaign' a shade loosely.

sense.evidence: "Mr. Ford sang out" for exclaimed, "his first big crack at it" for first large venture, "chippin' in several old-time tunes" for contributing, "meant to rock up at the Tuesday night do" for was to have appeared: all fit. "let on" means reveal, a slight strain for a publicly announced campaign.

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian retelling: "For the do", "the missus", "due to front up in New York this mornin'", "And the hope, so they reckon".

register.evidence: A full retold-yarn voice, with no swearing (allowed, not required). The news structure is kept but every sentence is retold in the vernacular.

tone.evidence: Keeps the light, curious news-item tone, retold: "where he might just answer the call of the footlights and sign a vaudeville contract".

flow.evidence: Smooth: "But the plans got changed, and tonight " leads naturally into Grandpa Mellie. One clunky stretch: "for the Ford " before Americana "of such pieces that's bein' got ready for publishin'".

variety.evidence: Varied: "let on", "big crack", "the do", "sang out", "chippin' in", "rock up", "front up", "so they reckon". "do" appears twice.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the AP item, told by someone passing on the news: "Word last night was he'll be under the management of Tex Rickard".

problems.quote: Henry Ford's already let on he's on a mission
problems.why: Let on suggests revealing something private; the campaign was publicly announced.

problems.quote: of such pieces that's bein' got ready for publishin'
problems.original: of such pieces now being prepared for publication
problems.why: Clunky join carried over from the original's syntax.

B.summary: A complete, natural, fully Aussie retelling that keeps every fact and Ford's quote intact.

meaning.evidence: All facts survive, but with additions: "Henry Ford, the motor car bloke himself" (colour), "so the thing's not just him and the band" (a reason the original doesn't give), "Not bad for an old fiddler, eh?" (colour). "the plans went out the window" overstates 'plans were changed'.

sense.evidence: "He was meant to lob at the Tuesday night do" for was to have appeared, "sawin' away" for playing the fiddle, "cookin' up a barn dance" for planning, "give Henry Ford's push a leg-up" for further his purpose: all fit. "came straight back at 'em" for exclaimed fits as a retort.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural ("lob", "with the missus in tow", "Word got around"), but the narrator tags are stock: "Here's one for ya.", "So there ya go.", "Not bad for an old fiddler, eh?"

register.evidence: Full pub-yarn weight: asides to the listener, slang throughout, no swearing (allowed, not required).

tone.evidence: Keeps the light news item, nudged toward a raconteur's chuckle: "Not bad for an old fiddler, eh?" The change of voice is what the brief asks for.

flow.evidence: Reads well, though the asides chop it a little: "So there ya go. Out of the twenty-one quadrilles".

variety.evidence: Very varied: "big crack", "big do", "whittle it down", "sawin' away", "chippin' in", "lob", "went out the window", "in tow", "cookin' up", "leg-up".

essence.evidence: Clearly the Ford square-dance item, told as a yarn: "he might just answer the call of the footlights and sign on for a vaudeville contract".

problems.quote: so the thing's not just him and the band
problems.original: and to form a nucleus for the party
problems.why: Adds a reason not in the original.

problems.quote: But the plans went out the window
problems.why: Overstates a simple change of plans.

C.summary: The most yarn-like and most varied, with some stock narrator tags and a small invented reason.

meaning.evidence: Every fact survives in order, Ford's quote verbatim: "Henry Ford's first big crack at the campaign he's already announced", "was meant to turn up at the Tuesday night do", "Word last night was he'll be under the management of Tex Rickard".

sense.evidence: "sang out", "the do", "chippin' in", "front up", "push to get square dances goin' again": all fit.

authenticity.evidence: Natural throughout: "For the do, Mr. Ford's advertisin' for couples", "with the missus". Nothing stagey.

register.evidence: A strong Aussie retelling, though a few lines stay close to the wire copy: "It was added that puttin' on this dance was hoped to help". No swearing (allowed, not required).

tone.evidence: Keeps the news item's light tone: "where he might answer the call of the footlights and sign up for a vaudeville contract".

flow.evidence: Mostly smooth; one clunky end: "It was added that puttin' on this dance was hoped to help Henry Ford's push".

variety.evidence: Good spread ("big crack", "comes off", "the do", "sang out", "chippin' in", "front up"), "the do" twice.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the AP item retold: "Out of the twenty-one quadrilles, Mr. Ford explained, they'll pick four".

problems.quote: It was added that puttin' on this dance was hoped to help
problems.original: It was added that in putting on this dance it was hoped to further Henry Ford's purpose
problems.why: Stays close to the wire syntax and reads awkwardly.

D.summary: Faithful and natural, close behind B, a little more tied to the wire copy's syntax.

meaning.evidence: All the reported facts survive, but Ford's direct quotation is rewritten and given a swear: "What we're trying to do putting out a book of dances is standardise the bloody things." Putting words in a real person's quoted mouth changes the record. "Mr. Ford fired up" shades 'exclaimed' toward annoyance.

sense.evidence: "big crack", "put the word out in the papers" for advertising, "the bright lights" for footlights: fit. "fired up" suggests anger where the original is enthusiasm; "get folks keener" uses folks, more American than Australian.

authenticity.evidence: Plain, natural casual English with some Aussie ("the Tuesday night do", "his missus"), but "get folks keener on 'em" is an Americanism.

register.evidence: Casual but light for level 5: "Mellie" Dunham gets into New York this morning. and "who's apparently planning a barn dance" are plain English. One mild swear within vulgarity 2 ("the bloody things").

tone.evidence: Ford's cheerful zeal becomes testier: "Mr. Ford fired up" and "standardise the bloody things".

flow.evidence: One stacked opening ("Right, so Henry Ford's first big crack at this campaign of his, the one he's already told everyone about, to teach the American public"), otherwise smooth.

variety.evidence: Some variety ("big crack", "put the word out", "chipping in", "the do", "bright lights"), lightly used.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the item, but the altered quote dents its character as a news report: "The first edition's being reworked to make it simpler."

problems.original: What we are trying to do in getting out a book of dances is to standardize them.
problems.why: Rewrites a real person's direct quote and adds a swear he didn't say.
Fired up suggests anger rather than enthusiasm.

E.summary: Natural but light, and it alters Ford's direct quote, adding a swear he never said.
